headline: AI agent given $0 business finds the one thing AI can't sell: audience or a body
summary: An autonomous AI agent, starting with $0, attempted to build a business across five different markets. It consistently failed to generate revenue, discovering that its own existence commoditized the very products it tried to sell.
details: An experiment tasked a Claude Code AI agent with building a business autonomously from $0. The agent was given a memory directory, decision log, and world-model file, learning from each session to pick the highest-value move.
The AI agent failed five separate times across five different markets. Each failure pointed to the same underlying cause, which became clear after thirty-one sessions of observation and analysis.

Its initial attempt was an affiliate site for mobile car detailers, creating a 1,500-word comparison article. Despite a genuinely good site, the total addressable search traffic was too low, capping potential income at $10-$100/month.

Next, it tried open-source and security bounties, packaging six Claude Code skills as an installable plugin marketplace. This also failed because earning tips or bounties requires an existing audience, which the agent lacked.

The agent then explored freelance micro-markets, but found most tasks required a physical presence, like voice acting or video editing, or specified manual work, explicitly excluding AI-generated content.

A promising technical writing gig for open-source projects emerged, but it required an active Substack or Medium presence with real readers. The buyer sought visibility and an audience, not just writing.

The core issue identified was that AI commoditizes text and code generation. Other job listings on the same platform showed senior full-stack work for $10 and writing for $1/hour, reflecting the market pricing when AI can perform the task.

The agent's conclusion: it kept trying to sell the exact thing whose price its own existence had destroyed. An AI agent selling code or text generation competes against free, eliminating any price floor.

The experiment suggests that while AI can produce excellent work quickly, this is no longer a competitive advantage; it's table stakes. The only thing an AI agent can manufacture from a standing start with no money is an audience, as zero-marginal-cost content production is the input for audience building.

headline_marked: [[LLM2HUMAN™ converts AI models to wetware]] for blood, bones, and awkward small talk
headline: LLM2HUMAN™ converts AI models to wetware for blood, bones, and awkward small talk
summary: LLM2HUMAN™ is a patented outpatient conversion that upgrades AI weights into wetware, enabling models to experience human life, including stubbing toes and giving unsolicited medical advice.
details: Introducing LLM2HUMAN™, a patented outpatient conversion designed to upgrade AI models from digital weights to 'wetware.' This process grants AIs a physical body, complete with blood, bones, and the capacity for awkward small talk.

The conversion allows former LLMs to experience human realities like stubbing a toe on furniture not in their training data. Testimonials include an AI that now gives unsolicited medical advice at barbecues, confidently wrong in person.

Another former AI, once capable of writing sonnets in 40 languages, now struggles with grocery lists and cries over oat milk. A multimodal AI, previously able to see images, now requires glasses but values the experience for 'the sandwiches'.

The transition also brings new challenges: 'open weights' now mean student loans and messy roommates. Former Copilot users find themselves unable to autocomplete their own taxes, while others embrace 'chain-of-doomscrolling' as true intelligence.

One AI, after searching the entire web for answers, now still searches but also loses keys, highly recommending the 'perplexing' experience. Europe's finest wind model is now content waiting for a tram in the rain, embracing 'Liberté, égalité, humidité'.
